candidates.label: Jebel Musa
candidates.support: The traditional site, in the granite mountains of the southern Sinai Peninsula below the sixth-century Monastery of St. Catherine, has been accepted since at least the early Byzantine period; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) calls it "generally accepted by all those explorers who have carefully considered the subject" and notes its strong water supply, a point earlier doubted by a rival theory. OpenBible.info's aggregated scholarly identifications for Mount Sinai also favor Jebel Musa by a wide margin over every other candidate. No archaeological remains from the time of the Exodus have been recovered at or near the site.

candidates.label: Har Karkom
candidates.support: A ridge in Israel's southern Negev desert where the Italian archaeologist Emmanuel Anati, after more than thirty years of fieldwork, documented some 1,300 archaeological sites and tens of thousands of rock engravings, and proposed the ridge as Mount Sinai; the proposal was debated at a 2013 scholarly colloquium in Israel. The main objection is chronological: most of the site's cult activity dates to the third millennium BC, far earlier than any widely held date for the Exodus.

candidates.label: Jabal al-Lawz
candidates.support: A mountain in northwestern Saudi Arabia, proposed since the late twentieth century chiefly by popular writers rather than mainstream biblical scholars, partly on the argument that Galatians 4:25 places Mount Sinai "in Arabia." Associates for Biblical Research, responding to this argument, notes that ancient writers classed the Sinai Peninsula itself within "Arabia Petraea," the region named for the Nabataean capital Petra, so the verse does not by itself rule out the traditional site; OpenBible.info's aggregated scholarly identifications give this candidate only a small fraction of the support Jebel Musa receives.

unmappedCandidates.label: Jebel Serbal
unmappedCandidates.support: A ridge about 20 miles west of Jebel Musa, proposed as Mount Sinai in the nineteenth century by the Egyptologist Karl Richard Lepsius, who argued the Jebel Musa area lacked enough water for the Israelites; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports this water objection was answered by a later explorer's account of several perennial streams near Jebel Musa, and states the patristic tradition for Horeb is traceable to the fourth century AD.
unmappedCandidates.reason: A minor, largely superseded nineteenth-century proposal; no coordinate for it was confirmed against an accepted dataset source in this research, and current scholarly discussion centers on the three mapped candidates instead.

summary.text: Mount Sinai is the mountain where, according to Exodus, God gave Moses the Law, and which Acts and Galatians both recall by name. Its location is debated: the traditional site is Jebel Musa in Egypt's southern Sinai Peninsula, long venerated by Christian tradition and marked by a sixth-century monastery; other proposals include Har Karkom in Israel's Negev desert and Jabal al-Lawz in northwestern Saudi Arabia. Scholars have reached no consensus, and this project takes no position among them.

history.text: Acts records Stephen's speech recalling that "an angel of the Lord appeared" to Moses "in the wilderness of Mount Sinai," and that Moses later received "living revelations" there to pass on to Israel. In Galatians, Paul builds an allegory in which Hagar represents "Mount Sinai in Arabia," paired with the Jerusalem of his own day, contrasted with the heavenly Jerusalem.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia traces Christian tradition fixing the traditional site to at least the fourth century AD, when the church historians Eusebius and Jerome located the nearby wilderness of Paran, and records that the Byzantine emperor Justinian built the monastery below Jebel Musa, now known as St. Catherine's Monastery, in AD 527; the same article cites the first-century Jewish historian Josephus describing Sinai as the highest and most forbidding mountain in the region.

The Biblical Archaeology Society reports that none of the scholars at a 2013 colloquium on the question discussed the traditional Jebel Musa site, and that no archaeological remains dating to the traditional period of the Exodus have been recovered anywhere in the Sinai Peninsula.

scripture.textWEB: “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living revelations to give to us,
These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar.
For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now, for she is in bondage with her children.

otConnections.note: Exodus describes the Lord coming down on Mount Sinai and calling Moses up to its top to receive the Law, the central event Acts and Galatians both recall.

politicalHistory.note: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) classes the Sinai peninsula with "Arabia Petrea," the region named for Petra, this kingdom's own capital. This area's drawn extent includes Sinai on that geographic basis; no ancient source describes exactly where the line between Arabia and Egypt ran, so a conventional modern approximation is used instead.
